YOGA-2018DEC-P2-Q89.question_text: Which of the following is not a component of the chitta?
YOGA-2018DEC-P2-Q89.passage: Maharshi Patanjali's Yoga Sutra has four padas or chapters: Samadhi Pada, Sadhana Pada, Vibhuti Pada and Kaivalya Pada. The Samadhi Pada describes the definition of yoga, the vrittis of the chitta and the kinds of samadhi. The chitta has three components: manas (mind), buddhi (intellect) and ahamkara (ego). Yoga is the restraint of the vrittis of the chitta, as a result of which the self attains its natural state. The vrittis of the chitta can be restrained through abhyasa and vairagya. The two main kinds of samadhi are sabija and nirbija samadhi. The Sadhana Pada describes kriya yoga, the five kleshas and the steps of bahiranga (outer) yoga. It describes the five yamas, five niyamas, asana, the four pranayamas and pratyahara, along with the benefits they bring to the practitioner. The yamas are called the great vow (mahavrata) because they are not limited by class, place or time. In the Vibhuti Pada, Maharshi Patanjali describes the steps of antaranga (inner) yoga: dharana, dhyana and samadhi. When these three are practised on the same object, they are together known as samyama. Dharana, dhyana and samadhi are outer limbs in relation to nirbija samadhi. This pada describes the transformations (parinama) of the chitta and the various kinds of vibhutis. The Kaivalya Pada discusses the five ways of attaining siddhis, the four kinds of karma and dharmamegha samadhi. Viveka khyati is the main means of attaining kaivalya. In the state of kaivalya the yogi is free of the purusharthas; the gunas merge back into their source, and the self returns to its own natural state.

YOGA-2018DEC-P2-Q95.question_text: In which kosha does avidya gradually diminish?
YOGA-2018DEC-P2-Q95.passage: In this age of modernisation, excessive speed and need-driven situations create imbalance and stress, which result in various kinds of disease. Imbalance at the emotional level, caused by strong likes and dislikes, shows itself as impulses. Imbalances at the psychological level give rise to conflict and often appear as narrow, ego-centred behaviour. At the subtle level, an unbalanced outlook and the lack of holistic knowledge are responsible for imbalance at the gross level. So, in understanding stress, the concept of the whole person should be kept in mind rather than mere physical existence. The Taittiriya Upanishad sets out the concept of the whole person systematically as five main sheaths, the pancha kosha. In modern medical science, stress is known and understood as an imbalance in the body's neuro-endocrine system. Emotional imbalance linked to strong likes and dislikes causes imbalance in the prana (vital energy) of the pranamaya kosha, which finally turns into stress and disease in the annamaya kosha. Desires that arise without considering right and wrong, and actions that follow from them, show up as imbalance in the manomaya kosha. In the vijnanamaya kosha avidya gradually diminishes, and in the anandamaya kosha it is transformed into bliss. This is the state of complete freedom from stress. Yoga is a boon for removing all the imbalances of life and attaining happiness and bliss.
